definition: Meager means deficient in size, amount, or quality — thin, small, and not enough.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word meager. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know meager should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The innkeeper served a meager dinner: a spoonful of rice and half a slice of bread.
A small lunch is simply not large; a meager lunch is too little to satisfy anyone.
A meager wage barely covers the basics; a pitiful one is so tiny it feels like an insult.

Paltry means so small it reads as an insult from whoever offered it — a paltry raise, a paltry settlement — and it sneers at the giver. Meager is sadder than it is angry: a meager meal or salary is thin and inadequate, but the word passes no judgment on anyone's generosity.

Skimpy means providing less than is needed, usually because someone cut corners — a skimpy portion, skimpy coverage. It hints that more could easily have been given. Meager describes plain inadequacy from any cause: a meager harvest after a drought skimped on nothing; there simply was not enough.

Insufficient is the neutral, technical way to say not enough for the purpose — insufficient funds, insufficient evidence. It states a shortfall without imagery. Meager adds the picture: thin, small, and inadequate, a word you can almost see. An account balance is insufficient; the dinner on the table is meager.

For a full week of hauling crates on the docks, the worker received a meager pay envelope that barely covered his rent.
Meager fits because the pay is far too small for the work done — deficient in amount, falling well short of what would be adequate.

Meager is a close cousin of scant, another word in this unit: both mean 'barely enough.' The nuance — meager stresses thin, inadequate quality or amount (a meager meal, a meager salary), while scant stresses falling just short of a needed amount (scant evidence, scant attention).
Meager pairs most naturally with food, money, and resources.

When Anza took over the branch library, the collection budget for the whole year was eight hundred dollars.
It was a meager sum for six shelves of children's books, a fact she never bothered to hide from the town council.
No one had shortchanged her on purpose; the county had split what little it had evenly, and every branch got the same thin slice.
Still, the arithmetic was plain: after replacing the picture books the toddlers had loved to pieces, four dollars remained for everything else.
She taped the budget to the door — not as an accusation, she said, but as a fact the town could look at.
